title_zh: 第二十一類 僧道騙

stories.title_en: A Monk Takes a Cow for His Mother

paragraphs.zh: 夏六月间，一行脚僧过于路，见小竖牧一伙牛。内有黄牝牛，大而肥。牧竖伸左脚与之舐，牝牛舐之；又与右脚与舐。僧问曰：“此牛何为舐你脚？”牧竖曰：“此牛最驯熟，吾甚爱之。我脚多汗咸，故牛爱舐。”僧知牛爱舐咸味，密此牛，系索长者家所畜的。
paragraphs.en: In the sixth month of summer a traveling monk was on the road and saw a herd-boy watching a group of cattle. Among them was a yellow cow, large and fat. The boy held out his left foot for it to lick, and the cow licked it; then he held out his right foot the same way. The monk asked, “Why does this cow lick your feet?” The boy said, “This cow is very tame. I am very fond of it. My feet sweat and taste of salt, so the cow likes to lick them.” The monk understood that cattle like a salty taste, and he quietly noted that this cow was one kept by Elder Suo.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，僧取浓盐汁，厚涂头脸及遍身手足等处，寻到索长者家，跪门涕泣曰：“愿赐慈悲心，超度我母子。”索老曰：“我不会说法念经，怎能超度人？”僧曰：“我先母在生，不肯修斋布福。今已死七年，知冥中必受罪谴，奈家贫不能功果追荐。因慕目连救母，情愿削发从师，专求度母。前月得遇善知识，指老母在长者家投生为黄牛母，敬来求超度。”索老曰：“我栏有四头牝牛，知何牛是？”僧曰：“愿同往看。畜物更有灵性，母子相见，必有恩爱情在，自与别的不同。”索老与僧同到栏前，放出群牛。僧见大牝牛到，即揭下袖蒂帽，涕泣跪向前曰：“此是吾母也！”牝牛嗅其咸味，以舌遍舐其头脸，若怜惜状。僧愈加流涕，又自剥去衣服，牛遍舐其身，不忍去。索老看见果异，真似母之爱子，但不能言耳。问曰：“既是你前生之母，今须何以超度？”僧曰：“我若有银，当以半价买去养，奈贫僧衣钵罄空。愿长者权舍贫僧，牵往山庵，日采草煮粥喂养。待其谴罪完满，天年数终，贫僧当收埋，念经卷超度，庶来世转身为人，不堕畜生道矣。”长者怜其词情恳切，曰：“吾舍与你去。”僧叩头拜谢，牵此牛往三日路外，付出庵寄养。
paragraphs.en: The next day the monk took thick salt brine and coated his head, face, whole body, hands, and feet with it, then found Elder Suo’s house. He knelt at the gate weeping and said, “Please show a compassionate heart and deliver my mother and me.” Elder Suo said, “I cannot preach or recite sutras. How could I deliver anyone?” The monk said, “While my late mother was alive she would not keep vegetarian fasts or give alms. She has been dead seven years, and I know she must be suffering punishment in the underworld, but our family is poor and I cannot afford the rites to save her. Admiring how Mulian saved his mother, I shaved my head and followed a teacher, seeking only to deliver her. Last month I met a good teacher who pointed out that my old mother had been reborn as a yellow cow in the elder’s house, so I have come respectfully to ask that she be delivered.” Elder Suo said, “I have four cows in the pen. How would one know which cow it is?” The monk said, “Please let me go and look with you. Beasts have even more spiritual nature. When mother and child meet, there will surely be affection, different from the others.” Elder Suo went with the monk to the pen and let the cattle out. When the monk saw the large cow arrive, he took off his cap, knelt forward weeping, and said, “This is my mother!” The cow smelled the salt and licked his head and face all over, as if pitying him. The monk wept still more, then stripped off his clothes himself; the cow licked his whole body and would not leave. Elder Suo saw that it truly was strange, just like a mother’s love for her child, only it could not speak. He asked, “If this is your mother from a former life, what must be done now to deliver her?” The monk said, “If I had silver, I would buy her at half price and raise her, but this poor monk’s robe and bowl are empty. I ask the elder to grant her to me for now. I will lead her to a mountain hermitage, pick grass each day, and cook gruel to feed her. When her punishment is complete and her natural span ends, I will bury her and recite sutras to deliver her, so that in the next life she may turn and become human and not fall into the animal path.” The elder pitied the earnestness of his words and said, “I grant her to you. Take her.” The monk kowtowed in thanks, led the cow three days’ journey away, and left her at a hermitage to be kept.

paragraphs.zh: 至十月，天气寒凉，叫屠子来宰，以一半分与，卖得价银一两五钱；一半僧自留，做成干粮，收藏衲袄中各处。径到索长者厅前，结双趺而坐。长者出曰：“何僧敢升厅而坐？”僧曰：“你颇认得我么？”长者曰：“不知你是何人，怎么认得？”僧曰：“亦自然觉得面熟么？”长者曰：“并无相会，何处面熟？”僧长叹曰：“你本来灵性且尽丧，何故不识故人色相！”长者曰：“何为是故人？”僧曰：“昔佛印点醒东坡，远公唤回乐天，非苏、白二公之故人乎？你前生与我同修，因尘心未断，复来享此人福。我今特来度你，急宜丢手尘债，再去勤修，庶不废前生功行也。”长者曰：“你安能识得前生？”僧曰：“我功行高你一倍。你今且享半生福禄，我又加半生苦修，何难知三生事因？”长者曰：“你今生若何苦修？”僧曰：“从前苦修且休提，现今已辟谷三年矣。”长者始惊曰：“你能辟谷，在我家辟一月何如？”僧笑曰：“三年于是，何有一月？”长者曰：“亦服茶汤乎？”僧曰：“清茶滚水，日一瓯耳。”长者留之，扫一空室与坐，早进瓯茶，夜进瓯滚水。
paragraphs.en: When the tenth month came and the weather turned cold, he called a butcher to slaughter her. He gave the butcher half, sold for one tael and five qian of silver; he kept the other half himself, made it into dried provisions, and hid them in various places in his patched robe. He went straight to Elder Suo’s hall and sat down in full lotus. The elder came out and said, “What monk dares come up into the hall and sit?” The monk said, “Do you rather recognize me?” The elder said, “I do not know who you are. How would I recognize you?” The monk said, “Do I not naturally look familiar?” The elder said, “We have never met. Where would the familiarity come from?” The monk sighed at length: “Your original spiritual nature is already lost completely. Why do you not know an old friend’s form?” The elder said, “What old friend?” The monk said, “In the past Foyin woke Dongpo, and Master Yuan called Letian back. Were they not old friends of Su and Bai? In a former life you cultivated together with me. Because your worldly heart was not cut off, you came back to enjoy these human blessings. I have come specially to deliver you. You should quickly drop worldly debts and go cultivate hard again, so as not to waste the merit of your former life.” The elder said, “How can you know former lives?” The monk said, “My merit is twice as high as yours. You are now enjoying half a lifetime of fortune, and I have added half a lifetime of bitter cultivation. Why would it be hard to know the causes of the three lives?” The elder said, “How have you bitterly cultivated in this life?” The monk said, “Never mind former bitter cultivation. I have already grain-fasted for three years.” The elder was startled at last: “If you can grain-fast, how about grain-fasting one month in my house?” The monk laughed: “Three years already—what is one month?” The elder said, “Do you still take tea and hot water?” The monk said, “Clear tea or boiling water, one bowl a day, that is all.” The elder kept him, swept an empty room for him to sit in, and sent in a bowl of tea in the morning and a bowl of boiling water at night.

paragraphs.zh: 连坐七日，再请出，答对如常。长者惊服，问曰：“我当如何修？”僧曰：“只弃家长往，自有修行善方。”长者曰：“妻寡子幼，产业付谁？此事不能。其次修何如？”僧曰：“唯有舍施，修寺奉佛，来生亦受福报。现今庐山一庵，化人独力修造。倘捐五百金，一完修之，亦一大功德也。”长者依言，遣仆同僧送五百金往，交付与住持明白，留仆住数日，送归报主。后僧分住持银二百五十两而去。其以辟谷动富翁，则私食所带之干粮耳，宁有人而真辟谷者！
paragraphs.en: He sat on like that for seven days, then was invited out again, and answered as usual. The elder was amazed and convinced, and asked, “How should I cultivate?” The monk said, “Just abandon the family and go far away; there are good methods of practice of themselves.” The elder said, “My wife would be left a widow and my children are young. Who would the property be given to? This I cannot do. What would the next-best cultivation be?” The monk said, “Only giving. Repair temples and serve the Buddha, and in the next life you will also receive blessed reward. Right now there is a hermitage on Mount Lu being rebuilt by one person’s donations. If you give five hundred taels and finish the repair in one stroke, that too is a great merit.” The elder followed his words, sent a servant with the monk to deliver five hundred taels, handed them clearly to the abbot, had the servant stay several days, then sent him home to report to his master. Later the monk split two hundred fifty taels of the abbot’s silver and left. As for moving the rich man by grain-fasting, he was privately eating the dried provisions he had brought. As if there were anyone who truly grain-fasts!

paragraphs.zh: 按：此僧脱牛，犹其小者，转卖之可也。名为生前母而宰食之，罪浮于天矣。至用为干粮而诈称辟谷，其骗亦大。虽半舍入庵，亦是好事，僧若得劝缘功。然周急赈贫，自当施于邻里，何必投入于庵？此愚人信福田利益之过也，亦未读傅奕公《高识传》矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: This monk’s stripping people of a cow was still the small part; he could have resold her. To name her his mother from her lifetime and then slaughter and eat her—the crime floats above Heaven. Then using her as dried provisions and falsely claiming to grain-fast: that swindle too was large. Though half the gift went into the hermitage, that was also a good deed, and the monk if he obtained the merit of urging the donation. But relieving the urgent and aiding the poor should of itself be given to neighbors. Why must it be thrown into a hermitage? This is the fault of fools who believe in the profits of the field of merit, and of not having read Master Fu Yi’s Gaoshi zhuan.

stories.title_en: Taking Infant Elixir to Fake Grain-Fasting

paragraphs.zh: 有僧自称能辟谷者，富家多召而试之。连七八日不食一粒，或间二三日，服滚汤一瓯而已。传名甚广，人争以金帛舍之。一乡官见褚县尊，偶道及此，称世间有此高僧，真仙佛再生于世出。褚公最正大，素不信僧道辈，曰：“人受此色身，哪能断绝食色？假托辟谷者，不过暗藏干粮，以哄惑愚民耳。明理君子，何可信此辈？若果能辟谷，彼将远遁深山，唯恐名落人间，何必浪游市里？受人施舍金帛，将何所用？”乡官被褚公一驳，似乎己为信邪，更欲取信其言，乃曰：“老父母不信，可召而试之，方知晚生言非妄矣。”
paragraphs.en: There was a monk who claimed he could grain-fast. Rich families often summoned him to test it. For seven or eight days running he would not eat a single grain, or every two or three days he would take only one bowl of boiling water. His name spread widely, and people competed to give him gold and silk. A local official, seeing Magistrate Chu, happened to mention this, saying the world had such an eminent monk, truly an immortal or Buddha born again. Master Chu was most upright, and had never believed monks and Daoists. He said, “People receive this physical body. How can they cut off food and sex? Those who pretend to grain-fast only hide dried provisions in secret, to fool the ignorant. How can a gentleman who understands principle believe this sort? If they could truly grain-fast, they would flee far into the deep mountains, fearing only that their names might fall among men. Why would they wander the markets? And if they accept gifts of gold and silk, what would they use them for?” The local official, rebuked by Master Chu, seemed as if he himself believed heresy, and wanted still more to make his words believed. So he said, “If Your Honor does not believe, you may summon him and test him, and then you will know this junior’s words are not false.”

paragraphs.zh: 褚公即差人唤至，令搜其身。别无夹带，唯持二十四个弥陀珠，诛之带入。扫一净室，布床席与坐，外遣人轮番密窥。日遣人明开门一视，出仍锁门。两日内，果结双趺而坐，容貌如故。第三日开视，见脸有乏汗，求滚水饮。褚公命与之，复出锁门。密窥者来禀曰：“僧以一弥陀珠调水饮讫，容貌复好。”后每两日进滚汤一碗，密窥者辄禀云：“以珠调吃。”
paragraphs.en: Master Chu at once sent men to call him in, and ordered his person searched. He had nothing else hidden on him, only twenty-four Amitabha beads, which they allowed him to bring in. They swept a clean room, spread a bed and mat for him to sit on, and outside sent people in rotation to watch in secret. Each day they sent someone to open the door openly and look once, then lock it again on leaving. For two days he did sit in full lotus, his looks unchanged. On the third day they opened and looked: his face had tired sweat, and he asked for boiling water to drink. Master Chu ordered it given, then they went out and locked the door again. The secret watchers came and reported: “The monk mixed one Amitabha bead in the water and drank it, and his looks recovered.” After that, every two days they sent in one bowl of boiling water, and the secret watchers always reported, “He mixed a bead and ate it.”

paragraphs.zh: 经十一日，召之出，取其弥陀珠视之，止十九枚在手耳。褚公收其珠，命收入轻监不许揽动，听彼静坐，以候发落。密嘱禁子曰。“铁容僧道人入见，两日后必问你乞食。你问其弥陀珠何以做？做来以水调之，与此珠一样，后重赏你。”
paragraphs.en: After eleven days they summoned him out, took his Amitabha beads and looked: only nineteen were still in his hands. Master Chu confiscated the beads, ordered him put in light detention and not to be disturbed, and let him sit quietly pending disposal. He secretly instructed the jailer: “Do not allow monks or Daoists to come in and see him. After two days he will surely beg you for food. Ask him how the Amitabha beads are made. If he makes some that, mixed with water, are the same as these beads, I will reward you heavily afterward.”

paragraphs.zh: 次日，僧即问禁子求食。禁子曰：“你教我作珠方法，便与你食。”僧曰：“此药极难得。你但与我食，出外多以银谢你，不必问此方。”禁子不与之食，三日饿倒，面青黄无人色矣。
paragraphs.en: The next day the monk asked the jailer for food. The jailer said, “Teach me the method for making the beads, and I will give you food.” The monk said, “This medicine is extremely hard to get. Just give me food. When I get out I will thank you with much silver. No need to ask for this formula.” The jailer gave him no food. After three days he collapsed from hunger, his face green-yellow, with no human color left.

paragraphs.zh: 褚公提出，审曰：“我早知此珠是孩儿丹矣。你供出制造方法来，免汝一死。”僧诈作将死形状，不敢应。褚公笑曰：“众看此辟谷僧，在褚爷前辟三日谷，即饿死矣。此丹妇人胎内孩子，必须谋死孕妇，剖其婴孩，以作此丹。不知你害死多少命，以造此恶业，你怎敢说出口？我岂求汝方乎？若打死你，罪还轻。”命衙前搭起一台，以十九枚珠发出，将四个调与众百姓看，以滚水调之，满碗都是膏液。有敢饮者，又香又甜，只饮两口，一日亦饱。后十五枚发与医生治补损。然后缚此僧在台上凌迟之。褚公曰：“县令为民父母，岂忍杀人？但为众冤泄恨矣。”众皆称快，而乡官后亦永不信僧道矣。
paragraphs.en: Master Chu had him brought out and examined him, saying, “I knew early on that these beads were infant elixir. Confess the method of manufacture, and I will spare you one death.” The monk pretended to be about to die, and dared not answer. Master Chu laughed: “Everyone look at this grain-fasting monk. Before Magistrate Chu he grain-fasted three days and is about to starve to death. This elixir is a child from a woman’s womb. You must plot to kill a pregnant woman and cut out the infant in order to make this elixir. Who knows how many lives you have destroyed to make this evil work—how dare you speak the formula aloud? As if I wanted your recipe? If I beat you to death, the punishment would still be light.” He ordered a platform built in front of the yamen, issued the nineteen beads, and had four mixed for the common people to see: mixed with boiling water, the whole bowl became a paste. Those who dared drink found it both fragrant and sweet; two mouthfuls and they were full for a day. The remaining fifteen were given to doctors to treat injuries and deficiencies. Then they bound this monk on the platform and put him to death by slicing. Master Chu said, “A county magistrate is father and mother to the people. How could he bear to kill? But this is to vent the hatred of the many wronged.” All called it satisfying, and afterward the local official never again believed monks and Daoists.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此诈辟谷者，多是藏干粮，其服孩儿丹者少。此粮非藏于身，恐人搜也。都寄于丐乞者之身，有人试之，则密以干粮付。又有服松毛竹叶者，松毛用羊蹄草同吃，竹叶用嫩蕨同吃，皆滑而可食。僧亦尝以此惑人，谓彼能服此。然从古有辟谷之说者，乃仙方，非人间所有也。曾见有遇异人授辟谷者，述之于左。
paragraphs.en: Note: Those who fake grain-fasting mostly hide dried provisions; those who take infant elixir are few. This food is not hidden on the body, for fear people will search. It is all entrusted to beggars’ bodies; when someone tests them, they secretly pass the dried provisions over. There are also those who take pine needles and bamboo leaves: pine needles eaten together with yangti herb, bamboo leaves eaten together with tender ferns, all slippery and edible. Monks have also used this to fool people, saying they can live on these. But from ancient times, the grain-fasting methods that exist are immortal recipes, not things of the human world. I once heard of someone who met an extraordinary person who taught grain-fasting; I record it below.

paragraphs.zh: 武夷山有贫民结庐于岩曲，仅容床灶，垦山种茶，卖以供食。积十数年，所开茶山，岁可收鬻三四金，每日力作不息，唯大寒、暑甚、风雨，终日寂坐岩庐下，不识经典，亦不通往来。
paragraphs.en: On Mount Wuyi a poor man built a hut in a bend of the cliffs, barely room for a bed and a stove. He opened the mountain and planted tea, selling it to feed himself. After ten-odd years the tea slopes he had opened could be harvested and sold for three or four taels a year. Every day he labored without rest; only in severe cold, extreme heat, or wind and rain would he sit silent all day under the cliff hut. He did not know the scriptures, and also had no dealings with others.

paragraphs.zh: 忽一日一道人过其庐，谓曰：“汝耕山劳苦，何不以茶山付人代耕，岁收一金，以买衣资？吾授汝辟谷方，则不须买米，不劳耕山，可安坐自足矣。”山民曰：“吾尝间修行人有辟谷方，若肯教我，愿拜师父求学。”道士曰：“你性子恬静，尽可修行。今后唯早晨煎清泉二罐，煎至半落，以两罐合煎作一罐，早午晚各饮二瓯。饮后澄心息想，以舌抵上颚，合口闭目，终日静坐。或天清神爽，爰出游，行则慢步闲观，随意所适，不拘半午，不拘片时。凡行住坐卧，只从心不拂。或山果草实可食者，遇着稍食一二不妨，但不可有意寻求。如此便可辟谷矣。记之不可轻易传人。”山民依此行之，一年果不食一黍，颜如金黄，轻健如常。同山旁居人，常不见其籴米，或过其庐，亦无锅甑。问之，答曰：“近年学得辟谷方。”居人转相传异。有拜之求方者，辄逃避不授，曰：“师嘱勿轻传泄。”次年传于远近，多有来册拜访者。或赍粮宿其居庐看守，至匝月，果唯见饮滚水，饮后静坐，寂无一为，亦无闲谈。不知者或穷问之，或与谈修养，微笑而起，出游山径，迨午晚归，复暖滚水而饮。凡人之来者不迎，去者不送，亦无半语讯问人。人问之，有可答者，随口答一二句。问其餘闲事，则摇首不应，若有厌烦之意，唯自去静坐。凡言动应酬，总是付之无心而已。第二年后，名益著。富家贵人，多备鞍轿迎者，坚逃不往。富贵人身往劝逼之，后亦遍往诸家，所到不食人一物，唯向空室静坐，若一木佛，然有言动而已。
paragraphs.en: Suddenly one day a Daoist passed his hut and said, “You till the mountain and labor hard. Why not give the tea slopes to someone else to till, take one tael a year to buy clothes, and let me teach you a grain-fasting method? Then you need not buy rice or labor at tilling, and can sit at ease and be sufficient.” The mountain man said, “I have heard in passing that practitioners have grain-fasting methods. If you are willing to teach me, I will bow to you as master and ask to learn.” The Daoist said, “Your nature is quiet; you are quite able to cultivate. From now on, in the morning only boil two jars of clear spring water down by half, then combine the two jars and boil them into one. Morning, noon, and evening drink two bowls each time. After drinking, still the mind and rest thought, press the tongue to the upper palate, close the mouth and shut the eyes, and sit quietly all day. Or if the sky is clear and the spirit fresh, then go out walking: walk slowly and look at leisure, following whatever suits you, whether half a day or only a moment. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying, only follow the mind and do not go against it. Or if there are mountain fruits and plant seeds that can be eaten, if you come upon them it does no harm to eat one or two, but you must not seek them on purpose. In this way you can grain-fast. Remember this, and do not lightly pass it to others.” The mountain man followed this and practiced it. After one year he indeed did not eat a single grain of millet; his face was gold-yellow, and he was light and strong as usual. People living on the same mountain nearby often did not see him buy rice; or if they passed his hut, there was also no pot or steamer. When they asked, he answered, “In recent years I have learned a grain-fasting method.” The neighbors passed the wonder from one to another. Those who bowed and asked for the method he would always flee and not teach, saying, “My teacher ordered me not to leak it lightly.” The next year it spread near and far, and many came with visiting cards to pay respects. Some brought grain and lodged in his hut to watch, for a full month: they indeed saw him only drink boiling water, then sit quietly after drinking, silent, doing nothing at all, and with no idle talk. Those who did not understand might question him hard, or talk with him of cultivation; he would smile, rise, and go walk the mountain paths, returning at noon or evening, then warm boiling water and drink again. Of people who came he did not welcome them; of those who left he did not see them off; he also did not ask people half a word. If people asked him, and there was something he could answer, he would answer one or two sentences offhand. If they asked about other idle matters, he would shake his head and not answer, as if annoyed, and only go sit quietly himself. All speech, movement, and social response he simply put down as no-mind. After the second year his name was still more famous. Rich houses and noble men often prepared saddles and sedan chairs to receive him; he firmly fled and would not go. When the rich and noble went in person to urge and press him, he later also went around to the various houses. Wherever he arrived he would not eat a single thing of theirs, only sit quietly in an empty room, like a wooden Buddha, with only some speech and movement.

paragraphs.zh: 经二年半后，有潭阳富人礼迎之，虔奉更肃，若敬神明。时进茶果，稍为食些少。后备清茶精饭，苦劝之食，坚辞不能，不得已为食一瓯。少顷饥甚，服滚汤。又饥饿不能禁，又索食。富人欢喜，肃进之。连三日内，皆一日五食，仅能止饥。山民自惊疑，急求归山，依旧服汤静坐，不免肚饥。后只得复食，三餐如寻常人矣。
paragraphs.en: After two and a half years a rich man of Tanyang received him with ceremony, serving him still more solemnly, as if honoring a god. From time to time he sent in tea and fruit, and the man ate a little. Later he prepared clear tea and fine rice and bitterly urged him to eat. He firmly declined that he could not; then, unable to help it, he ate one bowl. In a short while he was very hungry, and took boiling water. He was hungry again and could not bear it, and asked for food once more. The rich man was glad and served him solemnly. For three days running he ate five times a day, and only then could stop the hunger. The mountain man was startled and doubtful himself, and urgently asked to return to the mountain. He took water and sat quietly as before, but could not avoid a hungry belly. Later he had no choice but to eat again, three meals like an ordinary person.

paragraphs.zh: 按：山民所遇之道士，明是仙人。若辟谷三年完满，必有超度矣。惜哉为名所累，致人迎奉，致人逼食，而自毁前功。此劝食之愚。富人彼意，欲虔奉之，以分生佛之福，岂诚心奉道哉！此山民既为所误，而彼福亦安在也？且堕百劫之罪，来生必与山民结一大仇矣。观此，则辟谷乃仙方，不徒在服滚水静坐也。不然，后仍服之坐之，而何谷不能辟哉？则今之托辟谷索人钱米者，真盗贼僧道也。真辟谷者，敢令人知乎？
paragraphs.en: Note: The Daoist the mountain man met was clearly an immortal. If the three years of grain-fasting had been completed, there would surely have been deliverance. A pity he was burdened by fame, which brought people to receive and serve him, brought people to force him to eat, and he destroyed his former achievement himself. This was the folly of urging him to eat. That rich man’s intent was to serve him devoutly in order to share a living Buddha’s blessings. Was that a sincere heart serving the Way? This mountain man had already been harmed by it, and where then was that man’s blessing? He will also fall into the sin of a hundred kalpas, and in the next life he must form a great enmity with the mountain man. Looking at this, grain-fasting is an immortal method, not merely a matter of drinking boiling water and sitting still. Otherwise, afterward he still drank it and sat it—why then could grain not be fasted? So those today who plead grain-fasting in order to demand people’s money and rice are truly thief-monks and Daoists. Would a true grain-faster dare let people know?

stories.title_en: Believing a Monk’s Talk, He Nearly Came to Ruin

paragraphs.zh: 徽州人丁达，为人好善喜舍。一日，与友林泽往海澄买椒木，到临清等处发卖，货已卖讫。此处有一寺，内有名僧号无二者，年近三十餘，相貌俊雅，会讲经典，善谈因果，风动多少良家子弟，往寺参拜，常有被其劝化，削发出家者。时丁达邀林泽去谒无二。林泽曰：“你素性好善，闻此僧巧嘴善言，累诱人削发为僧。你若见之，被其哄惑，何以归见父母？”达曰：“劝在彼，从在我。我自有主，彼何能拿？”若要往拜之。见无二举动闲雅，谈及因果之事，达被打动，尽舍其财本，入寺拜无二为师，欲削发为僧。泽怒曰：“未到此处，我早言之。今果被哄惑，何以为人？”再三苦谏不听。泽自回去，达在寺修行。
paragraphs.en: Ding Da of Huizhou was a man who liked goodness and liked to give. One day he went with his friend Lin Ze to Haicheng to buy pepper-wood, and sold it at Linqing and other places; the goods were already sold off. In that place there was a temple, and in it a famous monk styled Wuer, nearly thirty-odd, of handsome looks, able to lecture on the scriptures and good at talking of karmic cause and effect. He moved any number of sons of good families to go to the temple and pay respects; often they were converted by him and shaved their heads to leave home. At the time Ding Da invited Lin Ze to go visit Wuer. Lin Ze said, “You have always liked goodness. I hear this monk has a clever mouth and good talk, and has repeatedly lured people to shave and become monks. If you see him and are fooled by him, how will you go home and face your parents?” Da said, “Persuasion is on his side; following is on mine. I have my own master within. How can he take me?” And he insisted on going to pay respects. He saw that Wuer’s manner was easy and refined, and when they talked of karmic matters Da was moved. He gave away all his trading capital, entered the temple, bowed to Wuer as his teacher, and wanted to shave his head and become a monk. Ze was angry: “Before we even reached this place I already said it. Now you have indeed been fooled. How can you still be a man?” He bitterly advised him again and again; Da would not listen. Ze went back by himself, and Da stayed in the temple to cultivate.

paragraphs.zh: 过二年后，僧无二因有董寡妇入寺烧香，容貌甚美，亦信善好念弥陀。带一使女，十七岁，国色娇媚，到寺亦参拜。无二以巧言劝诱，寡妇亦心服，即拜无二为师，欲削发为尼，暂在寺宿几夜。其丫头常往无二房送果吕，无二欲心难制，以白金十两戏之。丫头收其银，与之通情。无二又思及其嫠妇，夜潜入其房，候董氏熟睡，欲强奸之。董氏坚贞不从，喊曰：“何人无理，敢来奸盗？”言未数声，无二以手巾紧勒其颈，须臾而死。
paragraphs.en: After two years the monk Wuer, because Widow Dong came to the temple to burn incense—she was very beautiful, and also believed in goodness and liked to recite Amitabha. She brought a maid, seventeen, of national beauty and charm, who also paid respects at the temple. Wuer used clever words to persuade and lure; the widow’s heart also submitted. She at once bowed to Wuer as her teacher, wanted to shave her head and become a nun, and stayed a few nights in the temple for the time being. Her maid often went to Wuer’s room to deliver fruit. Wuer could not restrain desire, and used ten taels of white silver to sport with her. The maid took the silver and had relations with him. Wuer then thought also of the widow. At night he slipped into her room, waited until Dong-shi was in a deep sleep, and tried to rape her. Dong-shi was chaste and firm and would not comply. She cried out, “What person is so lawless, daring to come to rape and steal?” Before she had spoken many sounds, Wuer tightened a handkerchief around her neck, and in a moment she was dead.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，使女去报知董氏之子李英。及到寺，无二已先逃走矣。但无二久出名，各处人多认得。李英雇人遍处缉拿，不两日拿到送县。王爷即点民兵百餘，围绕其寺。时寺僧已四散逃命，无僧可拿。王爷再命焚其寺，将无二责了四十，问典刑之罪。
paragraphs.en: The next day the maid went and reported to Dong-shi’s son Li Ying. By the time they reached the temple, Wuer had already fled first. But Wuer had long been famous, and people in all places mostly recognized him. Li Ying hired men to hunt him everywhere; in less than two days they caught him and sent him to the county. Magistrate Wang at once mustered a hundred-odd militia and surrounded the temple. By then the temple monks had already scattered in all directions to save their lives; there was no monk who could be seized. Magistrate Wang further ordered the temple burned, had Wuer beaten forty strokes, and sentenced him to the capital penalty.

paragraphs.zh: 达悔财本俱丧，无颜回家。后家中已知达逃回，叫人寻觅归家，发长方敢出。此愚人信僧之明鉴也。
paragraphs.en: Da regretted that his capital was all lost, and had no face to go home. Later his family already knew Da had fled back, sent people to find him and bring him home, and only when his hair had grown long did he dare go out. This is a clear mirror of fools who believe monks.

paragraphs.zh: 按：寺门藏奸，僧徒即贼，此是常事，亦往往有败露者。人不目见，亦多耳闻，何犹不知戒？而妇人入寺，男子出家，真大愚也。董虽死犹幸完节；丁达虽幸逃生而财本已丧。使当时与无二并获，何分清浊？必并死狱中矣。故邪说引诱人者，无论士农工商，皆当勿信而远之可也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Temple gates hide villains, and monks are thieves. This is a common matter, and there are also often cases that come to light. If people have not seen it with their eyes, they have also often heard it with their ears. Why do they still not know to take warning? And women entering temples, men leaving home—truly great folly. Dong, though she died, was still fortunate to keep her chastity complete; Ding Da, though fortunate to escape with his life, had already lost his capital. If at the time he had been taken together with Wuer, how would they have told clean from dirty? He would surely have died in prison with him. So those who use heretical talk to lure people, whether scholar, farmer, artisan, or merchant, should all not believe it, and keep far from it.

stories.title_en: A Monk Who Looked Like the Guardian God Fakes a Subscription

paragraphs.zh: 天元寺年久倾颓，住持僧完朗有意修之，恐工费浩大，非有大力者发愿独任，未易举手。忽一日，游方僧若冰来寺投宿，身干魁梧，面方而黑，目圆耳长，宛似本寺伽蓝形象。完朗一见心喜，夜设斋款待，甚加勤敬。次日，僧若冰曰：“宝刹非兴旺，何如此肯接待十方？”完朗曰：“兴我寺者，在尊宿一臂之力，敢大有所托。”若冰曰：“山家缘薄，怎能相助？”完朗曰：“此寺须五百金方可全修，虽化些少众缘，亦不济事。看尊相，极似我本寺伽蓝，托你择巨富家，若化其全修，待彼在允否间，约其来寺亲看，我自有方法纳之。”
paragraphs.en: Tianyuan Temple had been dilapidated for years. The abbot Wanlang meant to repair it, but feared the labor and cost would be huge: unless some person of great power vowed to take it on alone, it would not be easy to raise a hand. Suddenly one day the wandering monk Ruobing came to the temple to lodge. He was tall and sturdy, with a square black face, round eyes and long ears, exactly like the image of this temple’s Qielan guardian. Wanlang was delighted at the sight, set a vegetarian feast that night to receive him, and treated him with extra diligence and respect. The next day the monk Ruobing said, “This precious monastery is not flourishing. Why then are you willing to receive the ten directions like this?” Wanlang said, “The one who will raise my temple is in your reverence’s one arm of strength. I dare greatly to rely on you.” Ruobing said, “This mountain household’s karmic ties are thin. How can I help?” Wanlang said, “This temple needs five hundred taels before it can be fully repaired. Even collecting a little from many donors will not serve. Looking at your honored appearance, you extremely resemble our temple’s Qielan. I ask you to pick a hugely rich family. If you collect from them for the full repair, wait until they are between agreeing and not, arrange for them to come to the temple and look in person, and I will have a method of my own to take them in.”

paragraphs.zh: 若冰会意，前去大江边，有柴商财本巨万。若冰备干粮在身，直到柴排厅中，朗讽一经，结趺而坐，高叫曰：“化缘！”柴商荆秀云命手下以钱与之。僧全不视，曰：“吾非化小可钱钞。贫僧与施主有夙缘，要化千金。”秀云作色曰：“化千金何用？”僧曰：“此去二百里，有天元寺。前创时，施主有缘在，故今生大富。近年颓坏，须五百金修理，又须五百金为香灯田，后可保长久，则施主功德远大矣。”秀云曰：“你为寺化疏，前生与此寺何缘？”僧曰：“寺本我居食之地，非有缘，得久居乎？”秀云不睬之。僧在柴排坐三日不去，手下人以饭与食，亦食；不与，亦不食。又过四日，秀云曰：“吾舍三百相助，你更去化别人。”僧曰：“有缘者不能化，无缘者何劳空说？”秀云曰：“你把疏簿来，我题三百两。”僧曰：“疏簿在寺中。三百亦不够用，不须题？你图今生享福，只施五百两。若布来世津梁，非千金不可。”秀云曰：“吾不信今生来生，你且领三百两去，好心修造。不足者，岂无别善人相助？”僧曰：“吾哪要银？你自送与住持僧。”秀云曰：“吾十日后送到寺来。”僧遂合掌，念“阿弥陀佛”一声而去。归对完朗详说其事，又约“十日后柴商且来，吾远避之。”完朗大喜，早备茶果斋品以待。
paragraphs.en: Ruobing understood. He went forward to the edge of the great river, where there was a firewood merchant with capital in the tens of thousands. Ruobing packed dried provisions on his person, went straight into the timber-raft hall, loudly chanted a sutra, sat in lotus, and called out, “Collecting alms!” The firewood merchant Jing Xiuyun ordered his men to give him cash. The monk did not look at it at all, and said, “I am not collecting paltry cash. This poor monk has a former-life tie with the donor, and wants to collect a thousand taels.” Xiuyun changed color: “What use is collecting a thousand taels?” The monk said, “Two hundred li from here is Tianyuan Temple. When it was first founded, the donor had a tie there, and so in this life you are greatly rich. In recent years it has fallen into ruin. It needs five hundred taels for repairs, and another five hundred taels for incense-and-lamp fields; afterward it can be kept long, and then the donor’s merit will be far and great.” Xiuyun said, “You are collecting a subscription for the temple. What tie did you have with this temple in a former life?” The monk said, “The temple is originally the place where I live and eat. Without a tie, could I dwell there long?” Xiuyun paid him no attention. The monk sat on the timber raft three days and would not leave. The men gave him rice, and he ate; if they did not give it, he also did not eat. After four more days Xiuyun said, “I will give three hundred to help. You go collect from others besides.” The monk said, “If I cannot collect from the one with the tie, why waste empty talk on those without a tie?” Xiuyun said, “Bring the subscription book. I will write three hundred taels.” The monk said, “The subscription book is at the temple. Three hundred is also not enough to use. No need to write it. If you only seek to enjoy blessings in this life, just give five hundred taels. If you would lay a ford and bridge for the next life, nothing less than a thousand taels will do.” Xiuyun said, “I do not believe in this life and the next. You take three hundred taels and go, and kindly do the building. If it is not enough, will there be no other good people to help?” The monk said, “Why would I want the silver? You send it yourself to the abbot.” Xiuyun said, “I will send it to the temple in ten days.” The monk then put his palms together, recited “Amitabha Buddha” once, and left. He returned and told Wanlang the matter in detail, and also arranged, “In ten days the firewood merchant will come. I will stay far away.” Wanlang was greatly pleased, and early prepared tea, fruit, and vegetarian dishes to wait.

paragraphs.zh: 至第十日，秀云果带银同两仆来。完朗知是柴商，肃迎待茶毕，问曰：“施主高姓？”秀云曰：“姓荆。”完朗曰：“施主从哪里来？”秀云曰：“前约宝刹中化疏僧，今敬从江上来。”完朗沉吟曰：“山寺未曾化疏。”秀云曰：“十七日前，有僧在柴楼中坐七日，我许他今日来。”完朗曰：“本寺僧此半月内并无人出外者，必方僧诈托也。”即命作斋相待。秀云心疑怪：“若方僧诈托，何不前日即领银去？”只存在心，遍寺闲游。到伽蓝祠去，举头看伽蓝宛似前日僧形象。两仆亦指曰：“此伽蓝好似前日僧。”秀云看越惊异，心疑是伽蓝化为僧，以劝我修寺。即以祈曰：“前日僧若是你变的，求一圣。”即打一圣。又曰：“三百金已带来，祈保今年大利。”再一圣，又得一阳。又曰：“三百不够，若要五百，求一圣。”又得一阴。”又祝曰：“我心中已悟。若更要五百两香灯，求一圣。”果掷一圣。秀云拜谢讫，来就斋席，谓完朗曰：“须用银几何？”完朗曰：“久有意要修。前日叫匠人估计，要五百两方够，故不敢举。”秀云曰：“我前日许过三百两，今现送在此，明日更送二百两来添。若修完备，再舍五百两买置香灯田，永远奉佛。”完朗闻言大喜，合掌下拜。后依约舍完，若冰密分二百两而去。
paragraphs.en: On the tenth day Xiuyun indeed brought silver and came with two servants. Wanlang knew it was the firewood merchant, received him with ceremony, finished serving tea, and asked, “What is the donor’s honored surname?” Xiuyun said, “Jing.” Wanlang said, “Where has the donor come from?” Xiuyun said, “I previously arranged with the subscription monk of this precious monastery. Now I have respectfully come up from the river.” Wanlang pondered: “This mountain temple has not been collecting subscriptions.” Xiuyun said, “Seventeen days ago a monk sat in my timber loft for seven days. I promised him I would come today.” Wanlang said, “In this past half month none of this temple’s monks have gone out. It must be a wandering monk falsely claiming it.” He at once ordered a vegetarian meal prepared. Xiuyun thought it strange in his heart: if a wandering monk was falsely claiming it, why did he not take the silver that day? He only kept it in mind, and wandered the whole temple at leisure. He went to the Qielan shrine, raised his head, and looked: the Qielan was exactly like the monk of the other day. The two servants also pointed and said, “This Qielan looks very like the monk from before.” Xiuyun looked and was still more amazed, and suspected in his heart that the Qielan had transformed into a monk in order to urge him to repair the temple. He then prayed: “If the monk of the other day was you transformed, grant one holy cast.” He at once threw the blocks and got one holy sign. He said again, “I have already brought three hundred taels. Pray that this year there be great profit.” He threw once more, and got a yang. He said again, “Three hundred is not enough. If you want five hundred, grant one holy cast.” He again got a yin. He blessed again: “I have already understood in my heart. If you further want five hundred taels for incense-and-lamp, grant one holy cast.” Indeed he threw one holy sign. Xiuyun bowed his thanks, came to the vegetarian feast, and said to Wanlang, “How much silver must be used?” Wanlang said, “I have long meant to repair it. The other day I had craftsmen estimate: it will take five hundred taels to be enough, so I dared not start.” Xiuyun said, “The other day I promised three hundred taels. I now deliver them here, and tomorrow I will send two hundred more to add. When the repair is complete, I will further give five hundred taels to buy incense-and-lamp fields, to serve the Buddha forever.” Wanlang heard this and was greatly pleased, put his palms together and bowed. Later Xiuyun gave it all as agreed, and Ruobing secretly took two hundred taels as his split and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：僧貌似伽蓝，故凑成此巧，亦可谓奇。然是人作成此套，何尝真有伽蓝化身乎！故富而能舍，本是善行；若谓真佛化缘而施舍者辄有福报，此两个装骗僧，岂能福人乎？吾不信也。
paragraphs.en: Note: The monk’s looks resembled the Qielan, so this trick was pieced together; one may also call it remarkable. But it was people who made up this setup. When was there ever a true Qielan incarnation? So being rich and able to give is originally a good deed. If one says that a true Buddha collecting alms, and those who give, always have blessed reward—could these two monks who staged a swindle bless anyone? I do not believe it.

stories.title_en: Falsely Claiming Foresight to Cheat a Silk Robe

paragraphs.zh: 东阳江达涧，父遗产万金。因为本府库吏累累浸润剥削，破去家产强半；又好男风，尝畜美好小仆，陪侍出入。有日，江之梁友遇其小仆，问曰：“前日为你相公买两匹青绢都长，做长衫必有剩。”小仆曰：“裁工不善做，先做一领太长，穿不得；后一领做得恰好。”梁曰：“长的可裁短，何妨？”仆曰：“他也不要得，已藏在书房大箱中去。”———原来江多衣服，其穿后不用的，都投入此箱。梁曰：“新服何忍弃，叫把与我修短服之。”仆曰：“你要问他讨，箱中第三件便是这新服。”
paragraphs.en: Jiang Dajian of Dongyang inherited ten thousand taels from his father. Because as a prefectural treasury clerk he was repeatedly soaked and pared away, more than half his family property was wrecked. He also liked male favorites, and often kept handsome young servants to attend him going out and in. One day Jiang’s friend Liang met his young servant and asked, “The other day two bolts of dark silk bought for your master were both long. Making a long robe there must be leftover.” The servant said, “The tailor was not good at the work. The first one he made was too long and cannot be worn; the later one was made just right.” Liang said, “The long one can be cut shorter. What harm?” The servant said, “He does not want it either. It has already been put away in the big chest in the study.”—Originally Jiang had many clothes; those he no longer used after wearing them were all thrown into this chest. Liang said, “How can one bear to throw away a new robe? Tell him to give it to me to alter shorter and wear.” The servant said, “If you want to ask him for it, the third piece in the chest is this new robe.”

paragraphs.zh: 适一僧在旁闻得，素知江达涧肯施舍，即诈称方僧，入江相公廨中抄化。江以两文钱施之。僧曰：“吾看满衙之中，皆有怨气，唯相公府中祥光满室，后日必有好官职，前程远大。吾将化你一件好服，以结个缘。”江曰：“我无好服。”僧曰：“你有一件穿不得的，舍与我好。”江故曰：“衣皆可穿，哪有穿不得的？”僧曰：“是一件新青绢太长的，在书房大箱中，第三件该舍与我，吾为尔消灾延寿。不然，你眼下有多少是非到。”江心异之，开大箱中看，果有两件在上，新绢服第三。便疑此僧先知，持出舍与之，问曰：“既舍此服，可免是非否？”僧曰：“我试你有善心否。今果肯施，便转灾成福矣。”
paragraphs.en: A monk standing nearby happened to hear this. He had long known that Jiang Dajian was willing to give, so he pretended to be a wandering monk and went into Master Jiang’s yamen quarters to collect alms. Jiang gave him two cash. The monk said, “I look through the whole yamen: there is resentful qi everywhere. Only in your honor’s residence auspicious light fills the rooms. Later you will surely have a good official post and a far future. I will collect one good robe from you, to form a tie.” Jiang said, “I have no good robes.” The monk said, “You have one that cannot be worn. Give it to me; that will be good.” Jiang therefore said, “The clothes can all be worn. How would there be one that cannot be worn?” The monk said, “It is one new dark-silk robe that is too long, in the big chest in the study. The third piece should be given to me. I will dispel disaster for you and extend your life. Otherwise you have much trouble arriving right before your eyes.” Jiang thought it strange in his heart, opened the big chest and looked: indeed there were two pieces on top, and the new silk robe was the third. He then suspected this monk had foresight, took it out and gave it to him, and asked, “Having given this robe, can I be spared the trouble?” The monk said, “I was testing whether you have a good heart. Now you are indeed willing to give, so disaster has already turned into fortune.”

paragraphs.zh: 按：今僧皆庸人，何能前知？其称已往事者，多得于传闻；说未来事者，皆涉于矫诬。观此僧欺江相公之事，则今之称善知识者，皆此类也。江相公之易欺如此，家安得不败？世之信僧引诱者，可以此为鉴。
paragraphs.en: Note: Monks today are all ordinary men. How can they know the future? When they speak of past events, they mostly get them from hearsay; when they speak of future events, they all involve false claims. Looking at this monk’s cheating of Master Jiang, then those today who call themselves good teachers are all of this type. Master Jiang was so easy to cheat—how could the household not fail? Those in the world who believe monks’ lures may take this as a warning.

title_zh: 第二十二類 煉丹騙

stories.title_en: Refining Elixir in a Deep Pit, with Long Stakes Set

paragraphs.zh: 古有炼丹之说，点铁成金，盖仙方，非人世有也。世所传炼丹之术，用好纹银三两，杂诸铅、汞辰、朱砂药物在炉同炼，每次须炼四十九日。至四十日后，须两人轮番守炉，昼夜不得暂时离守。丹成，可得九两，内除三两银本，要三两买药物，每次只出三两。一年可炼四次，共可得十二两，仅足供两人食用。故真得此方者，亦不屑为。其炼出丹银，亦可经煎，每次渐渐亏少，复归于无。但此银第二次不可为银母，若再炼，须另以纹银为母。此相传真方，费心费工，甚不易为。若云游方士，托炼丹为名以行骗者，用砒霜、雄黄诸物，炒好银为灰砂，假称曰“丹头”；然后将此与好银同煎，仍煎成银，彼便道“丹药可点成银”，此个个是弄假行骗之套子。
paragraphs.en: From of old there has been talk of refining elixir, pointing iron into gold. That is an immortal recipe, not something the human world has. The elixir-refining art transmitted in the world uses three taels of good fine silver, mixed with lead, mercury, chen-cinnabar, vermilion, and other drugs, refined together in a furnace. Each time it must be refined forty-nine days. After the fortieth day, two people must take turns watching the furnace, and may not leave it even for a moment, day or night. When the elixir is done, one can get nine taels. Inside that, subtract three taels of silver capital; it takes three taels to buy the drugs; each time only three taels come out. Four times can be refined in a year, twelve taels in all, barely enough for two people’s food. So those who have truly obtained this method also do not deign to do it. The elixir-silver that is refined can also stand further firing; each time it gradually lessens, and returns again to nothing. But this silver cannot be used as mother-silver a second time. If you refine again, you must use other fine silver as the mother. This is the transmitted true method: it costs heart and labor, and is very hard to do. As for wandering recipe-men who plead elixir-refining as a name in order to swindle: they use arsenic, realgar, and such things to fry good silver into ash-sand, and falsely call it “elixir seed.” Then they fry this together with good silver, and it still fries back into silver, and they then say “the elixir drug can point into silver.” Every one of these is a setup of making falsehood and running a swindle.

paragraphs.zh: 有一道士，自称能炼丹者。先以银灰明煎出些与人看，人多疑信相半。一富人独信之，请至家炼。道士曰：“炼丹乃仙术，家中多秽浊，恐不能成。可于僻地开坑一丈四尺深，下仅可容一床一炉，在此处烧炼四十九日。一百两银母，可炼出三百两矣。”富人依言，于后门凿一坑，广八尺，深一丈四尺。道士入坑去，命用银十两买铅、汞辰、朱砂等来，先炼丹头，三日已讫。富人付银百两与炼，日吊下三餐饭与食，道人又命讨一手握的坚实圆木七只，每只三尺五寸长，作符；用大棕索一条，交横缚柴符上，日以大斧摧打柴符。富人每日往坑上看。至三十餘日，柴符渐渐打下，只有一尺在上，心料银将成矣。道士知一月之久，防守者必懈，夜以索一头系裹银药，一头系在腰，将七只长符，每二尺打一符于上，扳援而升，将银吊起，夤夜逃去。次早送饭，下无人接。以烛照之，不见道士矣。梯下看之，银都窃去，方知彼蹈符而上，明白被其窃骗也。
paragraphs.en: There was a Daoist who claimed he could refine elixir. First he openly fried some silver ash out to show people. People were mostly half doubtful, half believing. One rich man alone believed him, and invited him to his house to refine. The Daoist said, “Refining elixir is an immortal art. A house has much filth and turbidity; I fear it cannot succeed. You may open a pit in a secluded place, one zhang four chi deep, the bottom only enough to hold one bed and one furnace, and burn and refine there for forty-nine days. One hundred taels of mother-silver can be refined into three hundred taels.” The rich man followed his words, dug a pit behind the back gate, eight chi across and one zhang four chi deep. The Daoist went down into the pit, ordered ten taels of silver used to buy lead, mercury, chen-cinnabar, vermilion, and the rest, first refined the elixir seed, and finished it in three days. The rich man handed over a hundred taels of silver to refine. Each day they lowered three meals for him to eat. The Daoist also ordered seven solid round logs of a hand’s grip, each three chi five cun long, to serve as talismans; he used one thick palm-fiber rope, bound crosswise on the wooden talismans, and each day had them pounded down with a big axe. The rich man went to look at the pit every day. After thirty-odd days the wooden talismans had been gradually driven down, with only one chi still above. He figured in his heart that the silver was about to be ready. The Daoist knew that after a full month the watchers would surely slacken. At night he tied one end of a rope around the wrapped silver-and-drugs, and the other end at his waist; he took the seven long talisman-stakes, drove one in every two chi above, climbed up by them, hoisted the silver, and fled in the dead of night. The next morning when they sent food, no one below took it. They lit a candle and looked: the Daoist was gone. They put down a ladder and looked: the silver had all been stolen. Only then did they know he had stepped the talismans and gone up, and they had clearly been stolen from and swindled.

paragraphs.zh: 按：深坑煅炼，使人不疑其逃。然用符用索，已早为出坑之计。其使人不疑处，即其脱身处也。后人鉴此，尚以炼丹为可信否？
paragraphs.en: Note: Calcining in a deep pit made people not suspect he would flee. But using talisman-stakes and using a rope, he had already early made his plan for getting out of the pit. The very place that made people not suspect was his place of escape. Later people, taking warning from this: can they still take elixir-refining as something to be believed?

stories.title_en: Believing in Elixir-Refining, He Brought Harm on a Whole House

paragraphs.zh: 方士以炼丹脱剥，受骗者历来无算，故明人皆能灼见其伪，拒绝不信。有一邴道士，术极高，拐一脚，明言已得真传炼丹术，不肯轻易为人炼。其法以丹头与人，任其以铜铅同煎，皆成银。彼自用则不须炼，但随手取出，都是银。或见人疾苦者，在手掌一捻，即取银与之；或衣袖中随来，亦是银。多肯施舍与贫人，由是，人称为“半仙”。有用银器皿设盛席待之者，食毕，令取一米桶置席上，以手取银器，件件收入桶中。及看，则空桶无一物，明言我收去不还矣。人以善言求取，则云：“已在你家内原藏器之所。”视之，果在。若恶言强取，则终不见。此谓得五鬼搬运之法。如此累显奇术，皆足骇动人。
paragraphs.en: Recipe-men use elixir-refining to strip people. Those swindled have from of old been beyond counting, so clear-sighted people can all see the fraud plainly and refuse it, not believing. There was one Daoist Bing, extremely skilled in arts, lame in one foot, who openly said he had already obtained the true transmission of the elixir-refining art, and would not lightly refine for others. His method was to give people the elixir seed, and let them fry it together with copper and lead: it all became silver. When he used it himself he did not need to refine; whatever he took out by hand was all silver. Sometimes, seeing people in hardship, he would pinch once in his palm and at once take out silver and give it; or it would come along from his sleeve, and that too was silver. He was often willing to give to the poor, and from this people called him “Half Immortal.” There were those who set silver vessels and a rich feast to receive him. When the meal was done, he had them take a rice bucket and set it on the table, and with his hand took the silver vessels, piece by piece, into the bucket. When they looked, it was an empty bucket with not one thing. He said openly, “I am taking them away and not returning them.” If people asked for them back with good words, he would say, “They are already in your house, in the original place where the vessels were stored.” They looked, and indeed they were. If they demanded them back with harsh words, then they were never seen again. This was called having obtained the method of the Five Ghosts’ transport. Strange arts displayed like this again and again were all enough to startle and move people.

paragraphs.zh: 有富人尧鲁信之，延至于家，朝夕参拜，敬礼备至，愿学其术。道士安然受拜，未肯遂传之。每日坐享其敬，饮醉而睡，睡醒而游，全不以其敬礼为意。但有甚术，凡拜之者便倾心悦服，与共席饮酒，使称颂其道。尧鲁一家老幼婢仆，皆尊敬之。唯鲁妻辛氏始终不信，累劝夫宜绝此邪人。后邴道士知之，以银二钱与其家小仆，曰：“你主母梳头时，可取她梳下头发一根与我。”小仆早晨取与之。道士得此发即作法，至半上午，辛氏中心只爱与道士通，谓婢曰：“今日我心异也。”至午益甚，又曰：“今日心中大异。”至半下午，心不能自禁，明谓侍婢曰：“吾往日极恶邴道士，今日何爱他好？你看我脸上何如？”婢曰：“你似欲睡模样。”至晚饭后，辛氏思与道士云雨之意极切，只恨一家人在旁耳。又强制住，密谓婢曰：“你今须紧跟我，或入道士房去，你须打我两掌，批我面皮，切不可忘。”及上床睡后，夫已睡着，辛氏披上衣，裸下体，开门径奔道士房去。道士正在作法催符。婢急跟出，呼曰：“此道士房，不可去！”亦不应。道士语婢曰：“你外去。”以手扯辛氏。婢近前批主母两颊，亦不管；又在面上打两掌，曰：“你未穿衣。”辛氏方醒，曰：“我是梦中来，何故真身在此？喜得你唤醒也。”手携婢曰：“快和我进去，好羞人也！”入房蹴夫醒，详言其情及得婢唤醒之事。夫曰：“哪有此理？你素恶他，故装此情捏之，岂有心既欲去，又肯叫婢挽之？这假话我不信。”次日，不得已述于夫兄言之。兄命弟逐去道士，亦不听；乃往县告之。县提去打二十，又会寄棒，打亦不痛，乃以收监。道士明是空身入监，随手取出都是银。以银贿禁子，令买酒肉入监食。禁子更加奉承，思求其方。后又解府解道，各官都加责，以无甚证据，不肯置之死。后竟托分上，放出逃去，不知所往。尧鲁一家长幼，后相继疾故，盖受其术所蛊也。唯辛氏贞正，寿考无恙，总理家政，以抚幼孙之长，至九十餘岁而卒。
paragraphs.en: There was a rich man, Yao Lu, who believed him. He invited him to his house, bowed morning and night, and paid respect to the full, wishing to learn his art. The Daoist calmly accepted the bows, and was not willing to transmit it at once. Each day he sat and enjoyed the respect, drank until drunk and slept, woke and wandered, and took no notice at all of the courtesy. But he had some art: whoever bowed to him would then pour out the heart and submit, drink at the same table, and be made to praise his Way. Yao Lu’s whole house, old and young, maids and servants, all honored him. Only Lu’s wife Xin-shi never believed from first to last, and repeatedly urged her husband that he should cut off this evil man. Later Daoist Bing learned of this, gave two qian of silver to a young servant of the house, and said, “When your mistress combs her hair, you may take one hair she combs out and give it to me.” The young servant took it in the morning and gave it to him. Once the Daoist got this hair he at once worked magic. By mid-morning Xin-shi’s heart only loved to have relations with the Daoist. She said to her maid, “Today my heart is strange.” By noon it was still worse, and she said again, “Today my heart is greatly strange.” By mid-afternoon she could not restrain herself, and said openly to the attending maid, “In the past I hated Daoist Bing extremely. Why do I love him today? How does my face look to you?” The maid said, “You look as if you want to sleep.” After the evening meal Xin-shi’s thought of coupling with the Daoist was extremely keen; she only hated that the whole family was beside her. She forced it down again, and said secretly to the maid, “You must now follow me close. If I go into the Daoist’s room, you must strike my two cheeks and slap my face. You must not forget.” After they had gone to bed and her husband was already asleep, Xin-shi threw on an upper garment, left her lower body bare, opened the door, and ran straight toward the Daoist’s room. The Daoist was just then working magic and urging the talisman. The maid hurriedly followed out and called, “This is the Daoist’s room. You must not go!” There was no answer. The Daoist told the maid, “You go outside,” and pulled Xin-shi by the hand. The maid came forward and slapped her mistress’s two cheeks; she still paid no heed. She struck her face two more times and said, “You have not put on your clothes.” Xin-shi then woke and said, “I came in a dream. Why is my real body here? Luckily you woke me.” She took the maid by the hand and said, “Quick, go in with me. How shameful!” She went into the room, kicked her husband awake, and told the matter in full, including how the maid had woken her. The husband said, “How could there be such a principle? You have always hated him, so you made up this scene to frame him. How could a heart that already wanted to go also be willing to tell a maid to pull you back? I do not believe this false talk.” The next day, unable to help it, she told it to her husband’s elder brother. The elder brother ordered the younger to drive the Daoist out; he would not listen either. Then he went to the county and accused him. The county summoned him, beat him twenty strokes, and also applied further beating with the rod; the beating also did not hurt, so they put him in jail. The Daoist clearly went into jail empty-handed, and whatever he took out by hand was all silver. He used silver to bribe the jailer, and had him buy wine and meat into the jail to eat. The jailer was still more deferential, hoping to seek his method. Later he was sent on to the prefecture and the circuit. Each official added beating; because there was not much evidence, they would not put him to death. Later he in fact used connections, was released, and fled, whereabouts unknown. Yao Lu’s whole house, old and young, later died of illness one after another; they were poisoned by his arts. Only Xin-shi, chaste and upright, lived long without harm, managed the household, raised the young grandsons to adulthood, and died past ninety.

paragraphs.zh: 按：妖术之暗中，如妖狐之投媚，必心邪而后能惑。苟心正者，虽入群妖之中，妖不能害。故傅奕不信死人之咒，而胡僧自死；仲淹下信杀子之鬼，而鬼自不来。辛氏心正，虽妖人灵法，能深疑于心，蚤嘱于婢，终不受其邪淫之毒。然则法虽巧，终不及人心之正也。后遇妖人者，其牢把心而勿睬之，彼邪亦安施哉？
paragraphs.en: Note: Heterodox arts striking in the dark are like a fox-spirit throwing itself to charm: the heart must first be evil, and only then can it be confused. If the heart is upright, even if one enters a crowd of demons, the demons cannot harm. Thus Fu Yi did not believe a curse that would kill a man, and the barbarian monk died of himself; Zhongyan did not believe a ghost that would kill a son, and the ghost never came of itself. Xin-shi’s heart was upright. Though a sorcerer’s magic could deeply disturb the mind, she early instructed the maid, and in the end did not suffer the poison of his lust. So though the method was clever, it finally could not match the uprightness of the human heart. Later those who meet sorcerers: hold the heart firm and pay them no mind. How then can their evil be applied?

stories.title_en: Elixir-Refining Hard to Shake: Poison Put in the Food

paragraphs.zh: 古潭一后生丁宇弘，机关伶俐，识尽世间情伪，人不能欺。偶遇一方士，自称能炼丹。宇弘早知其伪也，欲乘此以骗方士，故诈为不知之状而琐琐问之。方士曰：“丹是仙术，古来传于善人，专以济救贫穷者。先须采药炼成丹头，后用银一钱，与丹头同煎，可得三钱；一两可得三两。”宇弘曰：“更多可炼否？”方士曰：“只要有丹头，虽一百一千皆可炼。”宇弘先用银一钱与炼。方士加丹头三分，即煎出银三钱。宇弘喜，更以一两与煎，又得银三两。宇弘益喜，请方士到家，殷勤相待。及银已费尽，又求再炼添用，陆续炼出银三十餘两。惟以好言承奉之，愿学其术，终不多出银与炼，反将方士丹头之本骗来矣。
paragraphs.en: In ancient Tan a young man, Ding Yuhong, was sharp in devices and knew thoroughly the true and false of the world; people could not deceive him. He happened to meet a recipe-man who claimed he could refine elixir. Yuhong had long known it was false. He wanted to use this to swindle the recipe-man, so he pretended not to know and asked him in fussy detail. The recipe-man said, “Elixir is an immortal art, transmitted from of old to good people, specially to succor the poor. First you must gather drugs and refine them into elixir seed. Then take one qian of silver and fry it together with the elixir seed, and you can get three qian; one tael can get three taels.” Yuhong said, “Can still more be refined?” The recipe-man said, “So long as there is elixir seed, even a hundred or a thousand can all be refined.” Yuhong first used one qian of silver to refine. The recipe-man added three fen of elixir seed, and at once fried out three qian of silver. Yuhong was pleased, and further used one tael to fry, and again got three taels of silver. Yuhong was still more pleased, invited the recipe-man to his house, and treated him with great care. When the silver had already been used up, he asked to refine again to add more for use, and in succession they refined out thirty-odd taels of silver. He only used good words to wait on him, wished to learn his art, and in the end did not put out much silver of his own to refine. Instead he cheated over the recipe-man’s own capital in elixir seed.

paragraphs.zh: 方士思家中不奈他何，故说：“吾丹头已用尽。可多带银本，出外采药，再在外大炼。”宇弘明知其引外行骗，只自思“我用心提防，彼何以骗？”更欲尽骗其身心丹头之银，乃带银五十两，与俱出外，不肯取出费用。方士叫其取银买物，宇弘曰：“丹以换银，今已成之银，何必轻用？可取丹来炼银作路费，我银留买药。”方士尽将己丹头三两，宇弘用银十两，共炼成三十两，彼此各分一半。又远行两日，寝食严防。方士无计可脱，乃背地买砒霜在身，晚又买一鲜鱼入店。宇弘往煮熟，装作两碗，方士往捧一碗在席，放毒于内。又再捧一碗，故打忿嚏，将口馋溅入鱼上。方士曰：“这碗亵渎了，我吃。”及至半夜，宇弘腹疼。延至明晓，方士往医家求止疼药，煎服愈甚。至午，宇弘发散唇裂，腹痛难当，心疑是方士投毒，哀求之曰：“吾止有银五十五两，你能救我命，尽半与你。”时弘已不能起床矣。方士取其银置己包袱内，近床以药与之曰：“吾游方人，将攒他人银。你好奸狡，反骗去我银五十两。今止多得你五两，吾自行善心，以此药与你，凭你命当生死何如。”遂负行李逃去。宇弘急命店主以药煎。有认得者曰：“此解砒霜药也。”连服几次，疼稍止。再求近店人医之，三日始得痊愈，银已全被方士夺去矣，只沿路乞食而归。
paragraphs.en: The recipe-man thought that in the house he could do nothing with him, so he said, “My elixir seed is already used up. You may bring more silver capital, go out to gather drugs, and then refine in a large way outside.” Yuhong clearly knew this was luring him out to swindle, but only thought, “I will take care to guard. How can he swindle me?” He wanted still more to cheat him of all the remaining silver in the elixir seed, so he took fifty taels of silver and went out with him, and would not take it out to spend. The recipe-man told him to take silver to buy things. Yuhong said, “Elixir is for exchanging into silver. The silver already made—why spend it lightly? You may take elixir and refine silver for travel costs. I will keep my silver to buy drugs.” The recipe-man used all his remaining three taels of elixir seed; Yuhong used ten taels of silver; together they refined it into thirty taels, and each took half. They traveled two more days. At sleep and meals Yuhong guarded strictly. The recipe-man had no plan by which to strip him, so behind his back he bought arsenic and kept it on him. That evening he also bought a fresh fish into the inn. Yuhong went and cooked it done, made up as two bowls. The recipe-man went and brought one bowl to the table, and put poison in it. Then he brought the other bowl, deliberately gave an angry sneeze, and splashed saliva onto the fish. The recipe-man said, “This bowl is defiled. I will eat it.” By midnight Yuhong had belly pain. It lasted until dawn. The recipe-man went to a doctor and asked for a pain-stopping drug; after it was decocted and taken, it grew still worse. By noon Yuhong’s lips had split and cracked, the belly pain was unbearable, and he suspected in his heart that the recipe-man had put poison. He begged him, saying, “I have only fifty-five taels of silver. If you can save my life, I will give you half of it all.” By then Hong could already not get out of bed. The recipe-man took his silver, put it in his own bundle, came near the bed, gave him a drug, and said, “I am a wandering man, meaning to gather other people’s silver. You are so cunning, and instead cheated away fifty taels of my silver. Now I only get five taels extra from you. I will of myself show a good heart and give you this drug. Whether your life is to live or die, that is as it may be.” Then he took his luggage and fled. Yuhong urgently had the innkeeper decoct the drug. Someone who recognized it said, “This is the drug that counters arsenic.” After several doses the pain slightly stopped. He further sought a doctor from people near the inn. After three days he began to recover. The silver had already all been taken by the recipe-man. He could only beg food along the road and go home.

paragraphs.zh: 按：知防炼丹，莫如宇弘。虽百计不能骗，反骗方士银本几尽，可谓巧极矣。然终被其投毒，银尽还讫，又多去五两，且几乎丧命。幸而得生，沿路乞食，亦劳且辱矣。方士炼丹，其可信哉？
paragraphs.en: Note: For knowing how to guard against elixir-refining, none was like Yuhong. Though a hundred plans could not swindle him, he instead swindled the recipe-man of nearly all his silver capital. One may call it extremely clever. Yet in the end he was poisoned: the silver was all returned, and five taels more were gone, and he nearly lost his life. Lucky to live, begging food along the road—labor and shame enough. Can a recipe-man’s elixir-refining be believed?

title_zh: 第二十三類 法術騙

stories.title_en: A Monk Fakes Reflections in Water and Plots Rebellion

paragraphs.zh: 僧術中有以法咒水密咒某人，心欲何事，後令人自取照之，各隨其心之所欲，自現其形。有米春元者，富過百萬，田連兩府，年逾五十，不思會試，唯安享豪華以為樂。妖僧聞其富，欲騙其厚利也，挾咒水之術，往叩其門，自言能望氣，每見此宅紫氣上沖，有鸞鳳之彩。此百代王侯之兆，當有立翊運之功、分河山之帶礪者。米春元未信。僧曰：「吾傳有秘術，以符咒水能知此生榮枯結果。人但齋戒三日，虔心來照，則今生是何成就，自現於水中。」米乃留此僧，令家下人各齋戒。
paragraphs.en: Among monastic arts there is one that uses a method of cursing water, secretly cursing a certain person: whatever the heart desires, afterward they have the person take and look at it himself, and each, following what the heart wants, has his own form appear. There was one Mi Chunyuan, rich beyond a million, with fields joining two prefectures, past fifty, with no thought of sitting the metropolitan examination, only taking ease and luxury as his pleasure. A demonic monk heard of his wealth and wanted to cheat him of thick profit. Carrying the art of cursed water, he went and knocked at his gate, saying of himself that he could watch qi: he always saw purple qi rising from this house, with the colors of simurgh and phoenix. This was an omen of kings and lords for a hundred generations; there should be those who would establish the merit of assisting the dynasty’s fortune, and share the rivers and mountains under pledges of enfeoffment. Mi Chunyuan did not yet believe. The monk said, “I have transmitted a secret art. With talismans and cursed water one can know this life’s glory and withering and its end. A person need only fast three days, come with a devout heart to look, and what this life’s achievement is will of itself appear in the water.” Mi then kept this monk, and ordered everyone in the household to fast.

paragraphs.zh: 至第三日，注大缸水於庭。僧密語咒水，令諸人自照。米照見戴丫天冠，穿蟒袍。幼子照之，亦同。長次二子，只紗帽圓領而已。米正室照，亦妃冠鳳袍。兩長婦照，唯珠冠翟服。米大異之，僅秘於心。
paragraphs.en: On the third day they poured a large vat of water in the courtyard. The monk secretly spoke a curse over the water, and had everyone look for themselves. Mi looked and saw himself wearing a forked heavenly crown and python robes. His youngest son looked, and it was the same. The two elder sons had only gauze hats and round-collared robes. Mi’s principal wife looked, and she too had a consort’s crown and phoenix robes. The two elder daughters-in-law looked, and had only pearl crowns and pheasant-patterned dress. Mi thought it greatly strange, and only kept it secret in his heart.

paragraphs.zh: 後與流寓枝鄉官宴會，談及時事，枝曰：「今併後匹敵，金注支庶。禍之萌，必始宮闈。異日不為文皇之蹀血，或為沂王府之反召。此魯嫠所深卹者。」米曰：「往者逆未萌而折，宸豪已發而摧。國家如天之福，風雨何搖於牖戶也？」枝曰：「不然。文靜以監豎倡唐，姚衍以胖僧興國。若輔之得人，成敗安可料也？」米曰：「縱中土有故，水國偏在海隅，必無憂亂離也。」枝曰：「亦難保。讖云『某地出天子，江南作戰場』，正可慮也。」米曰：「使宸豪復興於今，成敗當何如？」枝曰：「今承平馳兵，更甚於昔。向令宸豪不久淹南康，某都不詐應反戈，安至以銅鐘灰也？」米聞言心喜。
paragraphs.en: Later, at a banquet with Zhi, a local official living away from his post, they talked of current affairs. Zhi said, “Now after combining they stand as matched rivals, and the gold is staked on the junior branches. The sprout of disaster will surely begin in the palace. One day it will be either the Yongle Emperor’s trampling in blood, or the rebellious summons of the Prince of Yi’s household. This is what the widow of Lu deeply worried over.” Mi said, “In the past, rebellion was snapped before it sprouted, and Chenhao, once he had risen, was crushed. The state’s fortune is like Heaven’s. How can wind and rain shake door and window?” Zhi said, “Not so. Wenjing raised Tang by means of eunuchs; Yao Yan founded a state by means of a fat monk. If they obtain the right helpers, how can success or failure be predicted?” Mi said, “Even if the central lands have trouble, this watery country lies off in a sea corner. There is surely no worry of chaos and separation.” Zhi said, “That too is hard to guarantee. A prophecy says, ‘A Son of Heaven will come forth from a certain place; Jiangnan will be a battlefield.’ That is exactly what is to be feared.” Mi said, “If Chenhao rose again today, what would success or failure be?” Zhi said, “Now in long peace the troops have gone slack, still more than in the past. If in those days Chenhao had not lingered long at Nankang, and a certain capital had not falsely answered and then turned their spears, how would it have come to copper-bell ashes?” Mi heard this and was pleased in his heart.

paragraphs.zh: 又有一僧，能降神附童者，言往來禍福，如聲應響。米請降之密禱，以欲圖不軌事。神降曰：「金鍾興，玉氣旺，清福扶王帝業強。洪流掃蕩人安泰，裂土移宮鎮遠方。」米猶未決休咎，再求明報。降童喝曰：「此何事而敢絮叨也！」米不敢問，而未解神意。既而漁人於深淵得巨鐘，金色燁然。米以為瑞也，召枝某及二僧決謀逆，欲俟五月某日五更早，大小官俱出城送萬壽表，乃閉四門，伏兵城外，悉殲之。
paragraphs.en: There was also another monk who could bring down a spirit to possess a boy, speaking of coming misfortunes and blessings like an echo answering a sound. Mi asked him to bring it down and prayed in secret, about wanting to plot an unlawful matter. The spirit descended and said: “The golden bell arises, jade qi flourishes; clear fortune supports the king, the imperial enterprise is strong. A great flood sweeps clean, people are at peace; split the land, move the palace, garrison the far regions.” Mi still had not decided good or ill, and again asked for a clear report. The possessed boy shouted, “What matter is this, that you dare chatter on!” Mi dared not ask, and still did not understand the spirit’s meaning. Soon after, a fisherman in a deep pool got a huge bell, gleaming gold. Mi took it as an omen. He summoned Zhi and the two monks to decide on plotting rebellion, meaning to wait until a certain day in the fifth month, at the fifth watch in the morning, when officials great and small would all leave the city to send off the imperial-longevity memorial, then close the four gates, ambush troops outside the city, and wipe them all out.

paragraphs.zh: 至四更，兵卒供執事者早起，見城內伏兵處燈火異常，急報軍官調兵捕之。城中擾亂，又遣兵守城。見江中船無數，皆早炊飯。城上兵疑是助亂者，大呼曰：「某人謀逆，被捕獲斬首矣！」外伏者見內無號砲，城上有備，又聞呼喊聲，送表官皆不出城，知事必敗露，河邊數十號船，乘微明時各各逃散。後官以亂者作造謀反劫庫問，捕獲數十餘人，皆斬首。而首逆者，反以不知情為辭，只擬流三千里而死於道。
paragraphs.en: At the fourth watch, soldiers and those on duty rose early, saw unusual lamps and fires at the places of ambush inside the city, and urgently reported to the officers, who deployed troops to arrest them. The city was in disorder, and they also sent troops to guard the walls. They saw countless boats on the river, all cooking breakfast early. The soldiers on the walls suspected they were aiding the rebels, and shouted, “So-and-so has plotted rebellion, been captured and beheaded!” Those ambushed outside saw no signal cannon from within, the walls were prepared, and they also heard the shouting. The officials sending the memorial all did not leave the city. They knew the matter must have come to light. Dozens of boats by the river, taking the faint light, each fled and scattered. Later officials treated the rebels as having plotted rebellion and robbery of the treasury. They captured several dozen men, all beheaded. The chief rebel, on the contrary, used not knowing as his plea, and was only sentenced to exile three thousand li, and died on the road.

paragraphs.zh: 按：米春元年老巨富，已無心向功名，更何心圖王侯？止以咒水妖僧啟其端，降神妖僧決其志，又以枝某失職，怏怏釀成大逆。二僧已就誅，而枝某幸脫於網。天何緩討凶人哉？猶幸聖朝清明，小丑旋殄，固太平之洪福，亦此地民風素良善忠順，不當受此叛逆者之荼毒也。然信僧惑邪之禍亦酷矣。後人其深鑑之，其深戒之。
paragraphs.en: Note: Mi Chunyuan was old and hugely rich, already with no heart toward rank and fame—still less what heart to plot to be a king or lord? Only the cursed-water demonic monk opened the beginning, the spirit-descending demonic monk decided his resolve, and also Zhi, out of office, resentful, brewed a great treason. The two monks had already been put to death, and Zhi luckily slipped the net. Why is Heaven slow to punish the wicked? Still, fortunately the sagely court is clear and bright, and the petty rebels were quickly wiped out. This was truly the great fortune of peace, and also this place’s folkways have always been good, loyal, and obedient, and they ought not to have suffered the poison of these rebels. Yet the disaster of believing monks and being confused by heresy is also cruel. Later people, deeply take this as a mirror; deeply take this as a warning.

stories.title_en: Sorcery Sends a Dream, Then They Rob the House

paragraphs.zh: 老狐晝伏岩洞，夜出尋食草木之實。有偶於草木中吸得天地氤氳之情者，便有靈變，能幻化為美婦，以迷誘人，採人之陽精，以益其靈通。法師捕得而烹之。和尚如求得狐心，焙而乾之，熏以好香，於深山中構一草廬，以狐心奉祀於中，日誦諸般懺文經卷超度之，夜則群妖眾怪嗥者、呼者、悲者、泣者、叫者、嘯者、能為人言或蠻語者，千怪萬狀，於草廬外哀弔，極其淒涼。要極大膽之人，方敢中處。弔過七日，亦漸漸稀少。晝夜常誦經作法，備果食供奉。積至四十九日，然後焚了草廬，把狐心領回，香火祀之。如明日欲往見某人，先夜以錦囊盛狐心，置於心上，夜必夢婦人領之，先見其人：次日往拜其人，已夢中相會。後有所干求，人必以為異而多從之。此僧家騙化之一術也。
paragraphs.en: Old foxes hide by day in cliff caves, and at night go out seeking the fruits of plants. Those that happen among the plants to draw in the generative breath of Heaven and Earth then have spiritual change. They can transform into beautiful women to bewitch and lure men, taking a man’s yang essence to increase their spiritual power. When a ritual master captures one and cooks it, if a monk obtains the fox’s heart, he roasts it dry, fumigates it with good incense, builds a thatched hut in the deep mountains, and enshrines the fox heart in it. By day he recites all kinds of repentance texts and sutra scrolls to deliver it. At night then crowds of demons and monsters—those that howl, those that call, those that grieve, those that weep, those that shout, those that whistle, those that can speak human words or barbarian speech—a thousand strange forms, mourn outside the hut, extremely desolate. Only a person of the greatest courage dares stay in the middle. After seven days of mourning they also gradually thin. Day and night he constantly recites sutras and works magic, and prepares fruit and food as offerings. When it has accumulated to forty-nine days, he then burns the thatched hut, takes the fox heart back, and worships it with incense and fire. If tomorrow he wants to go see a certain person, the night before he puts the fox heart in a brocade bag and places it on his heart. At night he will surely dream a woman leads him, and he first sees that person. The next day he goes to pay respects to that person, and they have already met in a dream. Afterward, whatever he seeks, people will surely find it strange and often comply. This is one art of monks’ fraudulent collecting.

paragraphs.zh: 有富家羊老，生二子娶二媳矣。蓄積盈餘，極是慳吝，分文不肯施捨。忽夜夢兩高僧來化緣，次日果有兩僧到，容貌儼如夢中所會者，稱言：「你取財太急，人多怨氣。吾與你有夙緣，特來為你懺悔。」羊老信之，問：「懺悔當如何？」僧曰：「你合家當齋戒三日，再買果餅麵食及三牲豬羊肉，半葷半素，吾為你作法請將，誦經供佛，將生前罪過解釋，再祈後增福祿，便家門請吉，死後免墮矣。」羊老依言，齋戒買辦。
paragraphs.en: There was a rich house, Yang-lao. He had two sons and had already married two daughters-in-law. His stores were more than enough, but he was extremely stingy, and would not give a single cash. Suddenly at night he dreamed two eminent monks came collecting alms. The next day two monks indeed arrived, their looks exactly like those he had met in the dream. They said, “You take wealth too urgently. People have much resentful qi. We have a former-life tie with you, and have come specially to repent for you.” Yang-lao believed them, and asked, “How should the repentance be done?” The monks said, “Your whole family should fast three days, then buy fruit, cakes, flour foods, and the three sacrificial meats of pig and sheep, half meat and half vegetarian. We will work magic for you, invite spirit-generals, recite sutras and offer to the Buddha, dissolve the sins of your lifetime, then pray that afterward blessings and emoluments increase, so the household will be fortunate, and after death you will be spared falling.” Yang-lao followed their words, fasted, and bought the things.

paragraphs.zh: 至第三日，又有兩僧到，又留相助誦經。至晚，來一僧念咒燒符，降遣羊老自跳自喊，取利劍在手，指其妻、子曰：「此鬼也。」悉手刃之。又追殺二媳。媳求僧解勸。僧指羊老喝曰：「坐！」羊老遂提劍咬牙，昏昏而坐，不醒人事。四僧入，輪姦二婦訖，以索縛之。搜其家財幣，捆作四擔，夤夜逃去。
paragraphs.en: On the third day two more monks arrived, and were also kept to help recite sutras. That evening a monk came, chanted spells and burned talismans, and sent Yang-lao jumping and shouting. He took a sharp sword in his hand, pointed at his wife and sons, and said, “These are ghosts.” He cut them all down with his own hand. Then he chased and tried to kill the two daughters-in-law. The daughters-in-law begged the monks to intervene and persuade. A monk pointed at Yang-lao and shouted, “Sit!” Yang-lao then held the sword, grinding his teeth, sat in a daze, and was not conscious. The four monks went in, raped the two women in turn, then bound them with rope. They searched the house for money and goods, packed four loads, and fled in the dead of night.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，有人入其家者，見羊老被髮伏劍，睜眼語，急出呼眾入看。親眾群擁而入，羊老只說要殺鬼。眾向前奪去其劍，呼其名曰：「你何故如此？」羊老漸漸復蘇。人又問之，才知應曰：「吾夢見鬼多，正在此殺鬼，得你們叫我醒也。」及入後室，妻與子皆被殺。羊老大哭曰：「此我記得，殺三鬼在此，又趕殺二鬼婆，被僧攔開。」及入房，二婦皆捆在床，乃呼鄰婦來解之。各稱被僧所姦，金銀財帛皆收拾去矣。一家痛恨無窮，一邊收殮三尸，一邊遣人四路趕僧，皆趕上兩日路，並不見踪而還。
paragraphs.en: The next day someone who entered the house saw Yang-lao with hair loose, clutching the sword, staring and talking. He rushed out and called people in to look. Relatives crowded in. Yang-lao only said he wanted to kill ghosts. They went forward, took away his sword, and called his name: “Why are you like this?” Yang-lao gradually revived. People asked him again, and only then he answered, “I dreamed there were many ghosts, and was just killing ghosts here. You called me awake.” When they went into the back rooms, wife and sons had all been killed. Yang-lao wailed, “This I remember: I killed three ghosts here, then chased and tried to kill two ghost-women, and the monks blocked me.” When they went into the rooms, both women were bound on the beds. They then called neighbor women to untie them. Each said she had been raped by the monks, and the gold, silver, and goods had all been gathered and taken. The whole house hated without end. On one side they prepared the three corpses for burial; on the other they sent people on four roads to chase the monks. All chased two days’ journey, saw no trace at all, and came back.

paragraphs.zh: 按：羊老素慳吝，則為富不仁之事有矣。乃僧悚以怨氣，便信其說，而留以作福懺悔，則心先自疚故也。僧欲行術劫財，而先形於夢，此亦得狐心引夢之術而用之。彼夢謂高僧而反為劫僧，不信晝所為而信夜所夢，亦惑矣；不行善於平昔，而求懺悔於修齋，亦愚矣。今人多殘忍不仁，貪暴不義，而欲飯僧供佛，追修懺悔，何異羊老之覆哉！甚矣！惡不可為，而僧不可信也。鑑此當為之凜凜。
paragraphs.en: Note: Yang-lao was always stingy, so there were surely deeds of being rich without benevolence. Then the monks frightened him with resentful qi, he believed their talk, and kept them to make blessings and repent—because the heart first felt guilty of itself. The monks wanted to work arts and rob wealth, and first took form in a dream. This too was obtaining the fox-heart art of leading dreams and using it. He dreamed they were eminent monks, and they turned out instead to be robber-monks. Not believing what is done by day, but believing what is dreamed by night, is also delusion. Not doing good in ordinary times, but seeking repentance in keeping a fast, is also folly. Today many people are cruel and unbenevolent, greedy and unjust, yet want to feed monks and offer to the Buddha, pursue cultivation and repentance. How is that different from Yang-lao’s overturning? Extreme indeed! Evil must not be done, and monks must not be believed. Seeing this, one should tremble.

stories.title_en: The Face-Stroking Thief Abducts Young Boys

paragraphs.zh: 往年，京城中有幼童出外，嘗被人拐帶而去，尋之又無踪。後累累有之。人多見一僧，摩幼童之臉，則幼童隨之而行。既而尋，已失之。故京城盛傳謂之「摩臉賊」。時在京僧釋人多，未察其孰是也。
paragraphs.en: In past years, in the capital, young boys who went out were often abducted and taken away; when people searched, there was again no trace. Later this happened again and again. Many people saw a monk stroke a young boy’s face, and then the boy followed him and walked. When they searched soon after, he was already lost. So the capital widely called him the “face-stroking thief.” At the time there were many monks in the capital, and they had not yet made out which one it was.

paragraphs.zh: 忽宓富人，止生一子，出外不返，四下跟尋甚急，各處出賞帖曰：「有收留得者，賞銀二十兩；報信者賞銀一十兩。」四出掛帖出賞，終莫得下落。
paragraphs.en: Suddenly a rich Mi family, who had only one son, had him go out and not return. They followed and searched in all directions very urgently, and put out reward notices in all places: “Anyone who has taken him in, reward twenty taels of silver; an informant, reward ten taels of silver.” They hung notices and offered rewards in all directions, and in the end never got word of him.

paragraphs.zh: 住宓家小屋人班八，以淘街為生。一日，懶去掏街，往城外晦真庵閒遊，轉入後室，四旁周覽。忽破水障中一小士露頭來。班八認是宓家人，忙呼之曰：「家中四處尋你，何故在此？」宓子曰：「僧閉禁我在此，你快來救我！」班八看房門已鎖，恐一人難帶此子出，謂之曰：「你小心暫在此，我報你令尊知，即來取你矣。」飛跑而歸，報宓老曰：「令郎受禁在晦真庵中，速去救之。」宓老即招五十餘人，前後到庵。班八引至庵後房中，打開門，認出宓子，又搜出十數童輩，即令眾人捆住僧小山並同庵三人，都縛來狀送到官。
paragraphs.en: Ban Ba, who lived in a small house of the Mi family, made a living cleaning streets. One day he was too lazy to go clean streets, went outside the city to Huizhen Hermitage to idle, turned into the back rooms, and looked all around. Suddenly a small scholar’s head showed through a broken water-screen. Ban Ba recognized him as of the Mi household, and hurriedly called, “Your family is searching for you in all four directions. Why are you here?” Mi’s son said, “The monk has locked me in here. Come save me quickly!” Ban Ba saw the door was already locked, feared one man would have a hard time taking this boy out, and said to him, “Stay careful here a while. I will report to your father, and then come get you.” He ran home at flying speed and reported to Mi-lao: “Your son is imprisoned in Huizhen Hermitage. Go save him at once.” Mi-lao at once gathered fifty-odd men, and they arrived at the hermitage from front and back. Ban Ba led them to the back room of the hermitage, broke open the door, identified Mi’s son, and also searched out a dozen other boys. He then had everyone bind the monk Xiaoshan and three others of the same hermitage. They were all tied and sent with a complaint to the officials.

paragraphs.zh: 官先審問眾童曰：「汝等如何被引入庵？」眾童曰：「和尚以手摩我眼睛，便見兩邊背後都是猛虎毒蛇，將來咬人傷人，唯面前一條路清淨好行，我輩只向前走，便到此庵，被和尚幽閉住。」又問曰：「和尚留汝等在庵幹何事？」眾童曰：「可恨這禿子，不拘日夜，將我等做苦春，極是疼痛。若不從，便將大杖撻打。眾人怕他，只得從他所為。」又問曰：「先拐來的後必長大，都放在何處去？」眾童曰：「有病者有長大者，和尚說放他回去，未知後都回家否。」官再審僧小山曰：「你拐來眾童後，病的長的都放哪裡去？」僧不敢應。再問同庵三人，都云：「毒死埋訖。」官聞言大怒，將小山打四十，同庵者各打二十，曰：「此罪不容於死。」令鎖出衙門外，許失童之家君聚手毆，打得身無完膚，有割其陽塞於僧口者，半日而死。人莫不恨其淫而快其死。後將其庵焚之，拐帶之禍遂息。
paragraphs.en: The official first questioned the boys: “How were you led into the hermitage?” The boys said, “The monk stroked our eyes with his hand, and then we saw on both sides behind us fierce tigers and venomous snakes, coming to bite and harm people. Only the one road in front was clean and good to walk. We only went forward, and then arrived at this hermitage, and were shut in by the monk.” He asked again, “What did the monk keep you in the hermitage to do?” The boys said, “Hateful, this bald one. Day or night, he used us for his lust, which was extremely painful. If we did not comply, he would beat us with a big staff. Everyone feared him, and had no choice but to do as he wanted.” He asked again, “Those abducted earlier must later have grown up. Where were they all sent?” The boys said, “Those who were sick and those who had grown up, the monk said he sent them back. We do not know whether afterward they all got home.” The official then examined the monk Xiaoshan: “After you abducted the boys, where did you send the sick ones and the grown ones?” The monk dared not answer. He asked the three of the same hermitage again; they all said, “Poisoned and buried.” The official heard this and was greatly enraged. He had Xiaoshan beaten forty strokes, and those of the same hermitage twenty each, and said, “This crime cannot be allowed to live.” He ordered them locked out in front of the yamen gate, and allowed the fathers of the lost boys to gather and beat them with their own hands. They were beaten until no skin was left whole. Some cut off his genitals and stuffed them in the monk’s mouth. He died within half a day. There was no one who did not hate his lust and rejoice at his death. Later they burned the hermitage, and the disaster of abduction then ceased.

paragraphs.zh: 按：好男風者，禽瀆之行。此僧必有春意之方，非拐諸幼童，無以快其欲。又習得妖法，摩其眼睛則昏花見怪，故可誘引童男。其罪浮於天矣。積惡貫盈，眾戮其身，言之羞口舌，書之污簡牘，人誰不切齒之！世有負男子之軀者，其可襲此僧之惡行哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: Those who love male-male relations—this is the conduct of beasts. This monk must have had a lust-enhancing method; without abducting young boys, he had no way to satisfy his desire. He also learned demonic arts: stroking their eyes, they would see darkness and monsters, so he could lure boys. His crime floats above Heaven. When accumulated evil was full, the crowd killed him. Speaking of it shames the tongue; writing it stains the pages. Who would not grind their teeth? Those in the world who bear a man’s body—how can they follow this monk’s evil conduct?

title_zh: 第二十四類 引嫖騙

stories.title_en: A Father Seeks His Son and Falls into Whoring Himself

paragraphs.zh: 富人左東溪，止生一子少山，常帶千金財本，往南京買賣。既而入院毛月華，一年不歸。東溪問於人，知子以嫖故，因貪歡忘返，累以信促之歸。初猶回音，推託以帳未取完，後信往亦不答。東溪聞其財本已費過半矣，心中甚怒。欲自往尋之，又思空行費盤纏，乃帶三百金貨物，僱僕施來祿同往京尋子。
paragraphs.en: The rich man Zuo Dongxi had only one son, Shaoshan, who often took a thousand taels of trading capital to Nanjing to buy and sell. Then he entered the house of Mao Yuehua, and for a year did not return. Dongxi asked people, learned that his son, because of whoring, had grown greedy for pleasure and forgotten to come back, and repeatedly sent letters urging him home. At first there were still replies, putting it off on accounts not yet collected; later, letters went and there was also no answer. Dongxi heard that more than half the capital had already been spent, and was very angry in his heart. He wanted to go himself to find him, then thought that going empty would waste travel money, so he took three hundred taels of goods, hired the servant Shi Lailu, and went together to the capital to find his son.

paragraphs.zh: 人貨到京，早有人報知少山云：「爾父帶貨來賣，兼欲尋汝。」少山聞言甚悶，急呼其媽毛惜卿謀之曰：「家父特來催我歸，爾計能陷他亦嫖，則我在此可久；不然，今須與你別矣。」惜卿曰：「你但深藏其間，忽與相見，我自有理會。」即遣人邀前院荀榮媽來，託他巧為牢籠。榮媽許諾而去。
paragraphs.en: When the men and goods reached the capital, someone had already reported to Shaoshan: “Your father has brought goods to sell, and also wants to find you.” Shaoshan heard this and was very dejected. He urgently called his madam, Mao Xiqing, to plan, saying, “Father has come specially to urge me home. If you have a plan that can trap him into whoring too, then I can stay here long.
